newsitem.title: UK: UK's Blair talks tough to EU on border controls.
newsitem.headline: UK's Blair talks tough to EU on border controls.

text.p: Prime Minister Tony Blair said on Tuesday that Britain would not give up control over its borders at next week's European Union summit.
On the eve of talks in Paris with French President Jacques Chirac and less than a week before the Amsterdam summit, Blair said Britain could not compromise on its borders.
"For Britain it is essential -- and we will be demanding this -- that we retain legal control of our frontiers," he told France's TF1 television channel in an interview in London.

"In the way the rest of Europe wishes to cooperate in the areas of immigration and asylum and visa, we have to retain control over our own frontiers and we have to be able to cooperate as and when we wish but in the right and proper way."

Former Conservative prime minister John Major, ousted by Labour's landslide May 1 election victory, had pledged to veto any Amsterdam treaty unless Britain's control over its borders was made legally unassailable.
Blair has promised a more positive tone on Europe and this has already been noticed and welcomed on by Britain's EU partners.
But his aides said they were surprised that other EU states had apparently not taken to heart that the new British government was just as adamant on the issue of borders.
The government argues that Britain's island status, as well as different immigration problems due to its colonial history, make it a special case.
But aides said they did not want to start talking of vetos and opt-outs -- language remeniscent of the obstructive tone of Major's beleagured administration in its last months.
"It is not necessary to raise the stakes in way which could be seen as -- and could become -- counterproductive," said one senior official in Blair's Downing Street office.
But he stressed Blair would not compromise on this point. "We want legal protection written in the treaty so watertight it cannot be challenged in the (European) court," the aide said.
Blair gave the same message to Belgian Prime Minister Jean-Luc Dehaene in talks in London on Tuesday and he is due to talk to other EU leaders by telephone in the next few days.
Government leaders believe Britain can reach a satisfactory deal at the Amsterdam summit.

Foreign Secretary Robin Cook said on Monday: "Precisely because this government is not shouting No' to everything out of prejudice, we are listened to with respect when we do say No' to issues that threaten Britain's national interests."

In the TF1 interview, in which Blair spoke in part in French, apologising for not speaking fluently but joking he was at least trying, he also underlined the changes he has wrought in Labour since taking control in 1994.

"I describe the Labour party today as not being about state ownership or ever higher taxes or ever more regulation," he said. "The Labour party in Britain today is what I call a broad alliance of progress and justice."
